<comment datatype="string">YghZ is an L-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (L-GAP) reductase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18620424">Desai08</a>]; the enzyme is also able
to detoxify methylglyoxal at a low rate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12583903">Grant03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16077126">Ko05</a>]. YghZ defines the AKR14 (aldo-keto
reductase 14) protein family [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12583903">Grant03</a>]. 
<p>
L-GAP is not a natural metabolite and is toxic to <i>E. coli</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319747">Tang77</a>]. L-GAP is a substrate of both the glycerol-3-phosphate and hexose phosphate transport systems of <i>E.coli</i> K-12 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/319747">Tang77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6995450">Guth80</a>]. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18620424">Desai08</a>] postulate that the physiological role of YghZ is the detoxification of L-GAP, which may be formed by
non-enzymatic racemization of GAP or by an unknown cellular process.
<p>
Overexpression of <i>yghZ</i> allows a <i>tpiA</i> mutant to grow slowly on L-lactate as the source of
carbon. <i>tpiA</i> mutants lack triosephosphate isomerase (TIM), and are thus unable to grow under
conditions where gluconeogenesis is required [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18620424">Desai08</a>]. The YghZ protein does not possess TIM
activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18620424">Desai08</a>]. YghZ overproduction results in decreased sensitivity to methylglyoxal,
compared to wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12583903">Grant03</a>]. Growth of a <i>yghZ gloA</i> double mutant is inhibited by 0.3
mM methylglyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16077126">Ko05</a>].
<p>
Expression of <i>yghZ</i> is not increased in response to methylglyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16077126">Ko05</a>].
<p>
The crystal structure of the <i>E. coli</i> enzyme has been determined and was suggested to be a tetramer [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22393408">Totir12</a>]. However, others have found that the protein forms an octamer based on gel filtration and electron micoscopy studies [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23103600">Lapthorn13</a>] (author statement).
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18928248">Richard08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23103600">Lapthorn13</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">The physiological function of the GldA enzyme has long been unclear.  The enzyme was independently isolated as a glycerol dehydrogenase and a D-1-amino-2-propanol:NAD<sup>+</sup> oxidoreductase.  At that time, D-1-amino-2-propanol was thought to be an intermediate for the biosynthesis of vitamin B12, and although <i>E. coli</i> is unable to synthesize vitamin B12 <i>de novo</i>, enzymes catalyzing the synthesis of this compound were sought [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4577583">Campbell73</a>].  It was later found that GldA was responsible for both activities [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3920199">Kelley85</a>].  
<p>
The primary <i>in vivo</i> role of GldA was recently proposed to be the removal of dihydroxyacetone by converting it to glycerol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18179582">Subedi08</a>].  However, a dual role in the fermentation of glycerol has also recently been established [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18632294">Gonzalez08</a>].  Glycerol dissimilation in <i>E. coli</i> can be accomplished by two different pathways in <i>E. coli</i>.  The <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY0-381">glycerol and glycerophosphodiester degradation</a> pathway requires the presence of a terminal electron acceptor and utilizes an ATP-dependent kinase of the Glp system, which phosphorylates glycerol to glycerol-3-phosphate.  However, upon inactivation of the kinase and selection for growth on glycerol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/197059">St77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6361270">Jin83</a>], it was found that an NAD<sup>+</sup>-linked dehydrogenase, GldA, was able to support glycerol fermentation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6183251">Tang82</a>] (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=GLYCEROLMETAB-PWY">glycerol degradation V</a>).  Recently, [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18632294">Gonzalez08</a>] showed that GldA was involved in glycerol fermentation both as a glycerol dehydrogenase, producing dihydroxyacetone, and as a 1,2-propanediol dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD<sup>+</sup> by producing 1,2-propanediol from acetol.
<p>
The enzyme is found in two catalytically active forms, a large form of eight subunits and a small form of two subunits.  The large form appears to be the major species [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/359547">Campbell78</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/40950">Tang79</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6361270">Jin83</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6365902">Kelley84</a>].
<p>
Kinetic modeling and metabolic control analysis suggested that glycolytic flux during glycerol fermentation is controlled by GldA and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=CPLX0-2081">dihydroxyacetone kinase</a>.  Overexpression of GldA and DhaKLM increased glycerol utilization and ethanol synthesis, suggesting the potential for industrial scale production of ethanol from crude glycerol [<a href="http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1096717608000578">Shams08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21858785">Cintolesi12</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24584248">Wong14</a>].
<p>
Conversely, a broad survey of aldehyde reductases showed that GldA was one of several endogenous aldehyde reductases that contribute to the degradation of desired aldehyde end products of metabolic engineering [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25108218">Rodriguez14</a>].
<p>
Expression of <i>gldA</i> is induced by hydroxyacetone in stationary phase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8132480">Truniger94</a>].
</comment>

<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-GLYOXAL">Methylglyoxal</a> is produced in small amounts during glycolysis (via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE">glycerone phosphate</a>), fatty acid metabolism (via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETONE">acetone</a>), and protein metabolism (via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AMINO-ACETONE">aminoacetone</a>). <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-GLYOXAL">Methylglyoxal</a> is highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10597025">Kalapos99</a>] for a review).
There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal dehydrogenases.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
There are several pathways for the removal of methylglyoxal. In this pathway, methylglyoxal is reduced to acetol by the action of various enymes possessing <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G7558-MONOMER">L-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate reductase</a> activity. 
Most of the enzymes that have been characterized with this activity belong to the family of NADPH-dependent aldo-keto reductases (AKRs). For example, the human aldose reductase (EC 1.1.1.21) and aldehyde reductase (EC 1.1.1.2) are both capable of reducing methylglyoxal to acetol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537826">Vander92</a>]. Other mammalian AKRs that were shown to catalyze this reaction include AKR1, AKR1A, AKR1B1, AKR7, AKR7A2 and AKR7A5 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16919">Wermuth77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10510318">Oconnor99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12123834">Hinshelwood02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12604212">Hinshelwood03</a>].
<p>
Several <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-83333"><i>Escherichia coli</i> K-12</a> enzymes homologous to the mammalian AKRs have also been shown to catalyze the same reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9095467">Misra96</a>]. Overexpression of the aldo-keto reductase AKR14A1, encoded by the <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G7558">gpr</a> gene, leads to increased resistance to methylglyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12583903">Grant03</a>]. In addition, three other genes (<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G6967">yeaE</a>, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G7565">dkgA</a>, and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=EG11648">dkgB</a>) were shown to encode proteins with similar activities [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16077126">Ko05</a>].
All four proteins were purified, and shown to catalyze the reaction in vitro, in the presence of NADPH. A similar enzyme has been identified in cyanobacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16804176">Xu06</a>].
<p>
A variation has been found in the Saccharomycete fungus <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-1004253"><i>Cyberlindnera mrakii</i></a>, in which an NADH-dependent methylglyoxal reductase has been documented [<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bInoue92%5d">Inoue92</a>].
<p>
Prolonged incubations of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> cell-free extracts with methylglyoxal resulted in conversion of acetol to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PROPANE-1-2-DIOL">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16077126">Ko05</a>]. The enzyme proposed to catalyze this reaction is <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=GLYCDEH-MONOMER">L-1,2-propanediol dehydrogenase / glycerol dehydrogenase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6183251">Tang82</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3920199">Kelley85</a>]. A similar conversion has been observed in other microorganisms, such as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-1517"><i>Thermoanaerobacterium thermosaccharolyticum</i></a>
[<a href="/META/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bCameron86%5d">Cameron86</a>]. In bacteria <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PROPANE-1-2-DIOL">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol</a> is a dead-end metabolite and exits the cell rapidly [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2644239">Zhu89</a>].
<p>
The same reaction has also been observed in mammalian systems, where it is catalyzed by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=HS01502-MONOMER">aldose reductase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537826">Vander92</a>]. In mammals <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PROPANE-1-2-DIOL">(<i>S</i>)-propane-1,2-diol</a> is metabolized in the liver to L-lactate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537826">Vander92</a>].</comment>
